title: Turkey’s UN Climate Draft Omits Fossil Fuel References, Ignoring Core Global Warming Drivers
body:
The draft text that Turkey is poised to present at the closing session of the United Nations climate conference in Antalya omits any reference to “fossil fuels,” the primary driver of the planet’s warming, sparking criticism from environmental groups and raising doubts about the ambition of the final accord. Delegates from more than 190 nations will convene on Sunday to negotiate the language that will shape the next global climate framework, and the absence of the term has become a flashpoint in an already contentious summit.

Turkey, which will host the conference’s final week, has framed its proposal as a “balanced” document that emphasizes “climate resilience” and “energy transition” without naming the carbon‑intensive fuels that dominate global energy consumption. The wording, officials say, is intended to keep the text “inclusive” and avoid alienating developing nations that still rely heavily on coal, oil and gas for economic growth. Yet the omission has been seized upon by NGOs, youth activists, and several small‑state delegations as a sign that the negotiations are being steered away from the hard choices required to limit warming to 1.5°C.

Environmental advocates argue that the deliberate exclusion of “fossil fuels” undermines the spirit of the Paris Agreement, which calls for a rapid phase‑down of carbon emissions. “If the language doesn’t name the problem, it can’t name the solution,” said Elena García, spokesperson for the Climate Justice Network, during a press briefing in Antalya. “We are at a crossroads: either we confront the reality of fossil‑fuel dependence head‑on, or we continue to produce a hollow document that offers no concrete pathway to decarbonisation.”

The debate reflects deeper geopolitical tensions that have long shaped climate diplomacy. Wealthier, industrialised countries have pushed for language that would compel a swift reduction in coal, oil and gas use, while many emerging economies argue that such mandates could jeopardise development goals and energy security. Turkey’s own energy mix—still heavily reliant on coal and newly discovered offshore gas—places it in a delicate position, balancing domestic interests with the desire to be seen as a constructive host.

In recent weeks, the conference has seen a series of high‑profile protests and diplomatic stand‑offs. Youth climate activists from the Fridays for Future movement staged a sit‑in at the UN pavilion, demanding explicit references to fossil‑fuel phase‑outs. Meanwhile, the European Union, which has pledged to cut its net emissions by at least 55% by 2030, warned that any final text lacking clear targets could jeopardise its own climate financing mechanisms. Conversely, representatives from the African Group highlighted the need for “climate‑just” language that acknowledges historic emissions and provides adequate adaptation funding, rather than focusing solely on supply‑side measures.

Negotiators are now wrestling with a compromise that could insert a clause calling for “phasing down” rather than “phasing out” fossil fuels, a subtle shift that would allow for continued use under stricter regulations. Some experts caution that such semantic gymnastics risk diluting accountability. “The devil is in the details,” noted Dr. Karim Al‑Hussein, a senior fellow at the International Institute for Sustainable Development. “A ‘phase‑down’ can be interpreted as a slow, incremental process, which may not be sufficient to keep the temperature rise below 1.5°C.”

As the Antalya talks draw to a close, the world will watch to see whether the final document can reconcile the divergent priorities of climate ambition, economic development, and geopolitical realities. The absence of the term “fossil fuels” in the draft signals a pivotal moment: either the global community will find a way to embed stronger, actionable commitments within the existing framework, or it will settle for a consensus that may fall short of the urgent emissions cuts scientists say are necessary. The outcome will set the tone for the next decade of climate policy, influencing everything from national energy strategies to the flow of international climate finance.
